primaryKeyword: why backlinks are important in seo
h1: Do backlinks still matter? Yes — as a tiebreaker
metaTitle: Why Backlinks Are Important in SEO (Still)
metaDescription: Why backlinks are important in SEO, and where they stopped mattering. Links settle close contests between comparable pages. They can't save a bad one.
answer: Backlinks matter because Google still uses them to judge which of several comparable pages deserves the top spot. What they no longer do is promote a page that misreads the query. Links are a tiebreaker between candidates, not an entry ticket — which is why link budgets so often produce nothing.
takeaways: Links decide close contests. They don't create candidates. A page Google considers a poor match for the query isn't in the contest to begin with.
There are whole query classes — local, long tail, brand, freshness-driven — where links barely participate.
Google's link spam systems now mostly **neutralise** bad links rather than penalise the site. Paying for nothing hurts more quietly than a penalty does.
The diagnostic is free: if pages with fewer referring domains outrank you, links are not your problem.

sections.h2: What a link is actually doing in 2026
body: The founding logic hasn't changed. A link from one site to another is a citation, and citations are the closest thing the open web has to a reputation system. Google confirmed links as a signal decades ago and has never withdrawn that.

What has changed is where in the process links get consulted. Google first has to decide which pages are even plausible answers to a query — a judgement made on meaning, format, coverage and trust. Links contribute little to that stage. Then, among the plausible answers, it has to order them. That's where links do their heaviest work.

Which reframes the whole budget question. Money spent on links is money spent on winning a contest you have to qualify for first. Spend it before you've qualified and it does nothing measurable, which is exactly what most founders describe when they say link building didn't work for them.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.body: Content and relevance get you into the top twenty. Links, brand and internal structure decide where in the top ten you land. Neither substitutes for the other, and only one of them is sold aggressively.

sections.h2: Where links genuinely decide the outcome
body: These are the query types where two pages look equally good to Google and something has to break the tie. Links break it more often than anything else you can influence.

body: This list is longer than the one above, and it covers most of what a mid-size Indian business actually competes for. If your target queries live here, a link budget is the wrong allocation.
bullets: **Local pack results.** Proximity, profile completeness and reviews decide the three map slots. A hundred referring domains won't move you closer to the searcher. Covered properly in [what local SEO is](/answers/what-is-local-seo).
**Long-tail informational queries.** Frequently won by whichever page answers the specific question most directly. Sites with almost no external links win these constantly.
**Format mismatch.** If Google has decided a query wants a product page and you've published a blog post, links won't promote the blog post. It's not competing in the right class.
**Pages that aren't indexed.** No index entry, no ranking, no matter what points at it. Check before you spend.
**Brand and navigational queries.** Your own name. If you're not winning these, the problem is entity confusion or a competitor bidding on you, not authority.
**Fresh-intent queries.** News and trending topics where publishing speed and publisher authority outrank accumulated link equity.
**Thin or duplicated content.** Links to a page Google considers low-quality are wasted, and occasionally worse than wasted.

callout.title: The most common misdiagnosis we see
callout.body: A founder is told they need links because they're stuck at position 30. Pages stuck at 30 are almost never held back by links — that's a relevance or format problem. Pages stuck at 8 to 15 are the ones where links genuinely move things. Position tells you which problem you have.

sections.h2: Velocity, and what natural growth looks like
body: Link velocity is the rate at which new referring domains appear. There's no safe number, because the right rate depends entirely on what your business is doing — and that's the actual test. Google isn't checking your links per month against a threshold. It's checking whether the pattern has a cause.

A company that launched a product, published original research and got covered in three trade publications should show a spike. That spike has an explanation sitting right next to it. A dormant six-page site that gains 300 referring domains in a fortnight has no explanation, and the pattern is trivially detectable.
bullets: **Healthy:** steady accumulation that tracks your publishing and PR activity, with occasional spikes tied to something real.
**Suspicious:** a flat line for two years, then a vertical climb, then a flat line again. That's a purchase, and it looks like one.
**Also suspicious:** perfectly consistent growth — exactly 20 new domains every month for a year. Nature isn't that tidy. Subscriptions are.
**Worth knowing:** losing links is normal. Sites redesign, articles get deleted, publications fold. A profile that only ever grows is a profile being manufactured.

sections.h2: What Google's link spam systems actually do
body: The mental model most people carry is from 2012 — Penguin, manual penalties, sites vanishing overnight. That era ended. Google's current link spam systems, built on SpamBrain, are designed to **nullify** unnatural links: identify them, discount them to zero, and rank the site as though they never existed.

That's a meaningful change in what failure looks like. You don't get a warning. Traffic doesn't crater. You simply paid ₹2,00,000 for links that contribute nothing, and because there's no visible event, nobody tells you. Plenty of agencies keep invoicing for exactly this, and their reports still show the link count rising.

Manual actions still exist and still arrive with a notice in Search Console. They're rarer, and they usually follow a pattern somebody built on purpose — a large volume of obviously paid, obviously commercial-anchor links pointing at money pages.

Worth saying plainly: negative SEO by pointing bad links at a competitor is largely ineffective for the same reason. Google's systems have to assume any site can be attacked, so nullifying rather than penalising is the only sane design.

callout.title: How we handle links
callout.body: Links are roughly 20–30% of the hours on our SEO work, and they're earned through digital PR, data and expert commentary — not bought. We start at ₹75,000/mo, smaller sites from ₹40,000, and the guarantee is against your own trailing-90-day organic lead baseline, frozen on day one. See [how we approach SEO](/seo).

sections.h2: Links or content? A ten-minute diagnostic
body: Before approving any link budget, run this on your five most valuable target queries. It costs nothing and it settles the argument that usually gets settled by whoever is most confident in the meeting.
numbered: **Is the page indexed?** Check Search Console. If not, stop here — nothing else matters until it is.
**What position is it in?** Below 30, or not ranking: this is a relevance or format problem. Between 8 and 20: links are a plausible cause.
**Does your page format match the top five?** If they're all category pages and yours is an article, rewrite the page. No link fixes this.
**Compare page-level referring domains** — yours against each of the top five. Not domain-level totals, which are meaningless for this question.
**If any competitor outranks you with fewer**, links aren't your constraint. Something about their page is better and it's usually visible within two minutes of reading it.

**If all five have substantially more**, and your page genuinely matches intent, you've found a real link gap. Now a budget makes sense — and the argument for spending it on internal linking first is in [internal linking beats link building](/journal/internal-linking-beats-link-building).

faqs.q: Do backlinks still matter for SEO in 2026?
faqs.a: Yes, confirmed by Google and visible in any competitive result set. What's changed is their scope. They separate comparable pages rather than promote weak ones, and there are entire query classes — local, long tail, brand — where they contribute almost nothing to the outcome.

faqs.q: How many backlinks do I need to rank on page one?
faqs.a: There's no universal number, and anyone offering one is selling a package. The answerable version: check how many referring domains point at each page currently ranking one to five for your query, and treat the median as your target. Sometimes that's zero.

No, and the reason isn't only ethical. Google's link spam systems increasingly nullify paid links rather than penalise you, so the realistic outcome is that you pay and nothing happens. The same budget spent on something worth citing produces links that keep working.

faqs.q: Can competitors hurt me by building spam links to my site?
faqs.a: Rarely. Google's systems have to assume any site can be targeted, so they ignore suspicious links rather than punish the destination. If you genuinely see a coordinated attack alongside a ranking drop, the disavow tool exists — but it's a last resort, not a maintenance habit.

faqs.q: What's better — more links or better content?
faqs.a: Whichever one you're short of, and the diagnostic above tells you which. As a rule, businesses under ₹50 crore have a content and relevance problem they've misdiagnosed as a link problem, because links are easier to buy than judgement is.

faqs.q: How long do backlinks take to affect rankings?
faqs.a: Google has to crawl the linking page, index it, and factor the link in — typically days to a few weeks. The ranking effect then builds over months as links accumulate. A single link almost never produces a visible movement, which is why link work is judged quarterly, not weekly.
